President Bola Tinubu has called for increased concessional climate financing and lower borrowing costs for developing countries, warning that the global climate finance ambition of mobilising at least $1.3tn annually by 2035 must translate into affordable and accessible funding for vulnerable economies. Tinubu said the high cost of capital confronting developing countries was undermining their ability to implement climate programmes, strengthen resilience and accelerate the transition to cleaner energy. The President made the call in Nigeria’s national statement delivered by the Minister of Environment, Balarabe Lawal, at the resumed high-level segment of the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference in Antalya, Türkiye, on Tuesday. High-level meetings at the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) resumed on Tuesday, November 17, in Antalya, Türkiye, following the two-day Antalya Leaders’ Summit held on November 11 and 12. In his speech delivered before the COP 31 President, Murat Kurum and other heads of states, he urged the international community to ensure that the Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage provided timely and meaningful assistance to countries suffering the consequences of climate change. The demand comes amid growing concerns among developing countries over the gap between international climate finance commitments and the availability of affordable funding to implement national climate action plans. Tinubu said climate action must be aligned with the development priorities of individual countries, particularly in areas of energy access, food security, industrialisation, employment and improved livelihoods. He maintained that Nigeria’s energy transition must reflect its economic realities, insisting that the country would continue to expand renewable energy while using natural gas as a transition fuel to support energy security and electricity access. Nigeria remains committed to expanding renewable energy deployment while safeguarding energy security and improving access to affordable and reliable electricity. Natural gas will continue to serve as an important transition fuel within our energy mix,” he said. The President highlighted Nigeria’s adaptation efforts, including the submission of its National Adaptation Plan in September 2026, which outlines interventions in climate-resilient agriculture, early-warning systems and disaster preparedness for vulnerable communities. He said the plan incorporated climate risk analysis, economic appraisal, sector strategies and financing approaches to strengthen the country’s capacity to respond to climate-related challenges. On efforts to attract private investment into clean energy, Tinubu disclosed that Nigeria commercially launched a `$300m Distributed Renewable Energy Fund in September to mobilise capital for expanding access to reliable electricity. He added that the Federal Government was strengthening its national carbon market framework and exploring opportunities under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement to mobilise additional resources for domestic climate action. Article 6 provides a framework for countries to cooperate through carbon markets and other mechanisms to achieve their emissions-reduction targets under the global climate agreement. However, Tinubu argued that domestic initiatives alone would not provide the scale of financing required to address the climate crisis, calling for stronger international cooperation and more accessible funding mechanisms. “National initiatives alone cannot deliver the scale of transformation required. The global ambition to mobilise at least US$1.3 trillion annually in climate finance by 2035 must translate into accessible and affordable resources, particularly for developing countries. “We call for increased concessional financing and reduced costs of capital confronting developing economies. We must ensure that the Fund for responding to Loss and Damage delivers timely and meaningful assistance to affected countries,” he said. The President urged world leaders to make COP31 a turning point in the implementation of climate commitments, arguing that climate ambition must be matched with financing and measurable outcomes. “COP31 must mark a decisive turning point in the global climate response. We must strengthen the alignment between climate ambition, financing and implementation, ensure that investments translate into tangible benefits for communities and foster partnerships that deliver lasting and meaningful outcomes,” he stated. He reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to multilateral climate cooperation, urging participating countries to move beyond pledges towards practical interventions that would improve resilience and support sustainable development. “Let Antalya be remembered as the moment the world moved decisively from commitment to implementation, and from investment to resilience, prosperity and shared development,” Tinubu said. COP31, hosted by Türkiye in Antalya, has brought together governments, development institutions, climate negotiators, businesses and civil society organisations to deliberate on global climate action, including financing, adaptation, energy transition and the implementation of the Paris Agreement. The resumed high-level segment on November 17 and 18 provides an opportunity for ministers and senior government representatives to present their countries’ positions and push for political agreement on outstanding climate priorities. The resumption comes as negotiations enter a critical phase ahead of the conference’s November 20 closing date. Delegates are working to bridge disagreements over climate finance, adaptation funding, the transition away from fossil fuels, renewable energy and the proposed target of increasing electricity’s share of global energy use to 35 per cent by 2035.
